newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: African peacekeeper, child killed in Bangui clash.
newsitem.headline: African peacekeeper, child killed in Bangui clash.

text.p: A Senegalese soldier and a child were killed when an African peacekeeping force fought with army mutineers in the Central African Republic capital Bangui on Friday, the local Red Cross said.
Red Cross spokesman David Dofara told Reuters the soldier had been shot dead and a 12-year-old boy was killed by an explosion. He said eight other people were wounded, one seriously.

It was the first such incident since a failed attempt to reintegrate mutineers from the paramilitary gendarmerie into their units under a January 25 peace plan to end the country's third army mutiny in under a year.
A spokesman for the peacekeeping force, Captain Lamine Gueye, said shooting erupted when peacekeepers intervened to stop a group of former mutineers holding up a private vehicle.
But Parfait Mbaye, a spokesman for the disaffected troops, said there had been no attempted hold-up and the peacekeepers had tried to disarm former mutineers returning to their base.
The sound of gunfire could be heard until midday (1100 GMT). The streets of the riverside city were deserted and shops and businesses closed early.
Officials say talks have begun to find ways of reintegrating the gendarmes into their units as has been the case with other members of the armed forces.

A stand-off between members of President Ange-Felix Patasse's presidential guard and gendarmes who joined the mutiny prevented an earlier attempt to reintegrate the gendarmes into the unit on June 13.

The African force, which includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo, deployed in Bangui under a peace accord brokered by Mali's widely respected former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure in January.
It is a likely model for efforts to broker peace in Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo Republic where similar political and ethnic clashes broke out on June 5.
The first mutinies, in April and May 1996, began as protests over pay but became a movement to topple Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993.
The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed. French troops, in the country under a defence pact, restored order and handed over to the African force.
The mutineers are principally from the southern Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
